# Draft:Mariama J. Lockington

----
Mariama J. Lockington (born December 30, 1984) is an American poet, author, educator, advocate and transracial adoptee.
Early and Personal Life
Lockington was born in Atlanta, Georgia on December 30, 1984. She was flown to Denver, Colorado by a social worker at three weeks old. Her adoption was closed. She is a transracial adoptee, having been raised by white parents. Her parents were open about their troubles with fertility and their desire to have both adoptive and biological children. Her mother told Lockington that 1960's and 70's, her maternal grandparents had been denied the adoption of a young Black boy due to the fact that they were on government assistance.
Lockington is the oldest of four siblings. Her mother became pregnant with her younger sister Eva approximately two years after her adoption. When she was six years old, her parents adopted her younger brother Devan, and they adopted her younger sister when she was a junior in high school. Both of her youngest siblings are also transracially adopted.
Growing up, she had a bullmastiff named Luchea. As an adult, she has had Daushunds named Walter and Henry, (affectionately dubbed "Sir Henry").
Both of Lockington's parents are classical musicians. Growing up, she lived in 10 different U.S. states. She has kept journals since kindergarten and started creating books and storytelling in second grade, when "she wore shortalls and flower leggings every day to school".
She was homeschooled for a period of her childhood.
Reading she was provided included A Chair for My Mother, Mufaro's Beautiful Daughters, Amazing Grace by Mary Hoffman, the Sweet Valley High series, Anne of Green Gables, Hatchet, Island of the Blue Dolphins, Jane Eyre, The Bluest Eye, Beloved, Heidi, Sula, Harriet the Spy, The Baby-Sitter's Club, Nancy Drew and the The Boxcar Children. She has stated a liking of the musical Annie. She recommends See No Color by Shannon Gibney as an adoptee story. Authors of note for her are Audre Lorde, Octavia E. Butler, Toni Morrison,  Sylvia Plath, Sharon Olds, and Anne Carson. She has expressed enthusiasm for the Alvin Ailey Dance Theatre. She is a fan of Buffy the Vampire Slayer.
Lockington purchases lipsticks for pleasure.
Lockington cooks, boxes, sings karaoke, and takes care of houseplants.
Lockington is in talk therapy.
In 2015, Lockington married her wife Vanessa in San Francisco City Hall. In August of that year, the couple moved to Michigan, their first two-bedroom house. They drove across the country, and were threatened in Pennysylvania by the police officer who arrested Sandra Bland. She is currently based in Lexington, Kentucky.
Education
She learned the piano as a child, but picked flute as her instrument of choice. She went to Interlochen Arts Camp for the flute one summer, and for creative writing another. She participated in weekly slam poetry nights and memorized Naomi Long Madgettt's Her Story. Her parents came to Michigan for a national slam poetry competition, for which she had two main poems she considered. One was was a "self-portrait" referring to her mother as a Venus flytrap and her father as a colonizer, and the one she chose, which was about her family's vegetarianism and veganism up until she was eight years old.
She also attended Interlochen Arts Academy in her senior year of high school.
Lockington graduated from the University of Michigan in 2007 with a dual BA in African-American Studies and Creative Writing and Literature. She has a Masters of Education from Lesley University and an MFA in poetry from San Francisco State University, after which she briefly moved to New York City.
Career
With knowledge of Spanish from a course at the University of Michigan, Lockington worked as a teaching fellow for Citizen Schools in Oakland, California. She also worked as a program coordinator and, later, director of education for 826 National and 826 NYC. In Lexington, Kentucky, she works with the Kentucky YMCA Youth Association.
Lockington is the founder of the womanist project Black Unicorn Book Club..
According to a spotlight by the University of Michigan,"She has edited and contributed to many youth-centered book projects including: Be Honest and Other Advice from Students Across the Country (2011, The New Press), Growing Our Hearts and Brains: Poems on love, technology, and success (2014, 826NYC), Chicken Makes the Ice Cream Taste Better: Stories on Food and Community, (2015, 826NYC), and her co-authored lesson plan “The Science of Superpowers” is included in STEM to Story: Enthralling and Effective Lesson Plans for grades 5th-8th (2015, Jossey-Bass). She is a Bread Loaf Writers' Conference Alumni, Voices of Our Nation Arts Alumni, a Literary Death Match Champion, and she continues to teach writing all over the country."In August of 2016, her article "What A Black Woman Wishes her Adoptive White Parents Knew" was published and became trending on BuzzFeed News. In 2017, she said that:"This year my mom gifted me a box of mementos she’d saved of mine since I was in preschool. Inside were a number of DIY books I’d made, with cardboard covers and duct tape binding, crayon illustrations, and pages and pages of stories written in what I can now only describe as word-salad."Her poetry chapbook The Lucky Daughter was published by Damaged Goods Press in 2017. It received positive reviews from Anthony Frame and Samantha Duncan.
Her debut middle grade novel, For Black Girls Like Me (Makeda and the Georgia Belles was its rough title while being written), was published by Farrar, Straus and Giroux on July 30, 2019. It was Today Show's best kids book of 2019 and was given five starred reviews.
Her second middle-grade novel, In The Key of Us, was published by the same company on April 26, 2022. It became a Mike Morgan & Larry Romans Children's & Young Adult Literature Award honor book and was featured in the The New York Times.
Her YA debut, Forever Is Now, was published on May 23, 2023. It stemmed from Lockington's own panic attacks and insomnia in the midst of the Covid-19 pandemic and following the death of Breonna Taylor. The novel won the Schneider Family Book Award."Every book I write starts with a playlist. The Forever is Now playlist is heavily influenced by some quintessential Bay Area artists, like Zion I, Too $short, and Goapele, but it’s also a journey through moods— from sad, to angry, to joyful, and then to songs of resistance and love. I really enjoy thinking about the musical plot of a book, and even though I can’t draft to music with lyrics, often between writing sessions, I play a song from the playlist to help me get ready for the next scene or even just to have a little dance break in my office. While I no longer practice my flute or the piano, I believe my poetry and storytelling are heavily influenced by my musical background. The full Forever Is Now playlist will be printed in the final book, so readers can engage with the songs as they like."Lockington's second YA novel, ''I've Got My Love to Keep Me Warm , was released on October 14, 2025.
She has contributed to the anthologies This Is Our Rainbow: 16 Stories of Her, Him, Them, and Us (2021), When We Become Ours: A YA Adoptee Anothology (2023), and All The Love Under a Vast Sky 2025.
Her poems "cottonwood" "georgia in new mexico" "tumbleweed" and "DO YOU LOVE IT? I LOVE IT! I GOT IT AT ROSS!" were published in Prelude Magazine. “upon moving back to michigan i plant a garden ​& become re-acquainted with my sister” was published in Muzzle Magazine. “hummingbird music camp— summer, 1997” was published in Paper Darts Magazine. “night sweats” was published in Perigee— Apogee Journal. “mountains” was published in Bodega Magazine, Issue 49. “June 12, 2016” was published in Pulsamos: LGBTQ poets respond to the Pulse Night Club shooting, Glass Poetry Press. "dear sis”  #bozalta4blacklives, was part of Issue 2, Bozalta Journal.
"kneel" was published in the Colorado Review, 2017. "prunus persica" was published by Locked Horn Press in Read America(s): An Anthology. “''oakland, 2010” and  “courses” were published in Washington Square, Issue 36. “Georgia Slave Code, 1848” and “the lucky daughter” were published in Uncommon Core: Contemperary Poems for Learning and Living.
